title: The history of the pressure cooker
tagline: From a scientist's bone digester in 1679 to the whistle in every Indian kitchen.
intro: Denis Papin found that sealing a pot let water get far hotter than 100 °C, and that a weighted valve kept it from bursting. Canners, doctors and mountain cooks took up the idea. In the 20th century it became a home pot, and in India the weight valve's whistle became a kitchen clock.

eras.name: Papin's digester
eras.summary: A scientist in London seals a pot, cooks bones soft, and invents the weighted safety valve.

eras.name: Preserving and sterilising
eras.summary: Heat keeps food from spoiling. Steam pressure retorts and the autoclave take water above 100 °C in factories and laboratories.

eras.name: The home cooker
eras.summary: Pressure cookers go on sale, climb mountains, get rubber gaskets and safety plugs, and become saucepans.

eras.name: India's whistle
eras.summary: Indian makers start in 1959. The weight valve's whistle and the ISI mark become part of every kitchen.

eras.name: Sensors and electricity
eras.summary: Electric cookers swap the flame and the whistle for a heater, a sensor and a timer.

events.title: A pot that cooks above boiling
events.text: Papin, a French scientist working with Robert Boyle, showed the Royal Society his steam digester. Its lid was screwed down so tightly that steam could not escape, so the water inside got far hotter than 100 °C.
events.why: It is the first pressure cooker on record.

events.title: A weight on a lever: the safety valve
events.text: Early digesters could burst. Papin fitted a small valve held shut by a weight on a lever, so steam pushed it open before the pressure got dangerous. Sliding the weight along the lever set the pressure.
events.why: Every pressure cooker, boiler and steam engine since has a safety valve. Papin is widely credited with the first one, though one historian notes he was the first to print it rather than certainly the first to make it.

events.title: Papin joins the Royal Society
events.text: Papin was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, the scientific academy that had watched his digester work.
events.why: It shows how seriously the scientists of the day took a cooking pot.

events.title: A book on softening bones
events.text: Papin described the digester in a pamphlet usually titled "A New Digester or Engine for Softning Bones". He promised that the oldest, toughest beef could be made tender, and that bones would make good jelly.
events.why: It was the first printed account of cooking under pressure, with the first printed drawing of a safety valve.

events.title: A supper cooked under pressure
events.who: Denis Papin and members of the Royal Society
events.text: Papin cooked a whole meal in his digesters for Fellows of the Royal Society. The diarist John Evelyn wrote that bones came out as soft as cheese, and he took home a jelly made from beef bones.
events.why: It was a public test of the idea that pressure cooks food faster and softer.

events.title: From cooking pot to steam engine
events.text: Papin built a model of a piston moved by steam, the first of its kind. Steam under a piston pushed it up, and as it cooled and condensed the air pushed it back down.
events.why: The power of trapped steam, first seen in the digester, became the idea behind the steam engine.

events.title: Food sealed and heated keeps for years
events.text: Appert won a French government prize for sealing food in bottles and heating them in boiling water. In 1810 he published his method so anyone could use it.
events.why: Preserving food by heat led, later, to pressure retorts that heat it above 100 °C.

events.title: Pressure cookers made for sale
events.text: Gutbrod is said to have begun making pressure cookers of tinned cast iron, though the record of this is thin.
events.why: It is one of the first signs of pressure cookers as things to buy rather than laboratory devices.

events.title: A steam pressure retort for cans
events.text: Shriver patented a process for heating sealed cans of oysters, fruit and vegetables. He is often credited with bringing the steam pressure retort to canning, which heated cans above 100 °C without bursting them.
events.why: Pressure made canning faster and safer, and gave the first factories a reason to build big pressure vessels.

events.title: The autoclave sterilises with steam
events.text: Working in Louis Pasteur's laboratory, Chamberland built a steam pressure chamber to sterilise culture media and tools. Today autoclaves typically run at 121 °C, with steam at about 100 kPa gauge, for 15 minutes or more.
events.why: The same physics as a kitchen cooker became a standard tool of every hospital and laboratory.

events.title: A cooker for the mountains
events.text: Crook founded The Pressure Cooker Company and sold an aluminium home cooker to high-country communities in Colorado, where water boils well below 100 °C.
events.why: Altitude was one of the first reasons people needed a cooker at home, as it still is in Ladakh.

events.title: Aluminium canners for home kitchens
events.text: The firm, which had made canner retorts for factories, installed an aluminium foundry to make pressure canners for homes. In 1917 the US Department of Agriculture decided pressure canning was the only safe home method for low-acid foods.
events.why: Home canning carried pressure vessels into ordinary kitchens.

events.title: The olla exprés
events.text: Spain granted Alix patent number 71143 for a pressure cooker he called the olla exprés. In 1924 he published the first pressure-cooker recipe book, with 360 recipes.
events.why: The pressure cooker began to be sold as an everyday cooking pot.

events.title: A cooker that went to Everest
events.text: The Automa pressure cooker was introduced, and climbers took it to Mount Everest to cook where water boils at about 70 °C.
events.why: It showed the cooker as the answer to cooking at altitude.

events.title: A rubber safety plug
events.text: Vischer presented his Flex-Seal Speed Cooker and filed a patent for a pressure relief device: a flexible rubber plug in the lid that blows out if the pressure gets too high. The patent was granted in 1942.
events.why: The blow-out plug became a common backup to the weight valve.

events.title: The saucepan cooker
events.text: At the New York World's Fair the company showed the Presto, which it calls the first saucepan-style pressure cooker. A turning lid and a simple gasket replaced bolts and clamps.
events.why: The turning lid with a gasket is still how many cookers close today.

events.title: Back from the war
events.text: During the Second World War the company stopped making cookers and made fuzes and bombs instead. When production restarted in 1945, Presto says it sold more cookers than all eleven other makers put together.
events.why: After the war the pressure cooker became a mass-market kitchen tool.

events.title: A third of American homes
events.text: About 37% of US households owned a pressure cooker in 1950. By 2011 that had fallen to about 20%.
events.why: In America the cooker boomed and faded; in India it became nearly universal.

events.title: The cocotte-minute
events.text: SEB introduced its Super Cocotte, a pressed aluminium cooker with a clamp to lock the lid. It sold in great numbers in France.
events.why: It made the pressure cooker a household word in Europe.

events.title: Pressure cookers made in India
events.text: The company, founded in Madras in 1955, began making pressure cookers in 1959 with technical help from the Prestige Group of the United Kingdom.
events.why: Cookers made in India began their spread into Indian kitchens.

events.title: Pressure Cookers and Appliances Ltd
events.text: Vasudeva founded the company that became Hawkins Cookers, in technical collaboration with L. G. Hawkins and Co. of England. It was renamed Hawkins Cookers Ltd in 1986 and says it has sold over 110 million cookers.
events.why: The whistle of the weight valve, and counting it, became part of daily life in India.

events.title: The electric pressure cooker
events.text: The first electric pressure cookers appeared in 1991. A heater, a pressure sensor and a controller replaced the flame and the whistle. One extension source names the inventor as a Chinese scientist, Yong-Guang Wang.
events.why: It moved pressure cooking from the stove to the counter, with no flame to watch.

events.title: The multicooker craze
events.text: A small Ottawa company launched an electric multicooker that combined a pressure cooker, slow cooker and rice cooker, and sold it online.
events.why: It brought pressure cooking back to many homes in North America.

events.title: The ISI mark becomes compulsory
events.who: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
events.text: The government ordered that every domestic pressure cooker sold in India must meet IS 2347 and carry the BIS Standard Mark. After an amendment, the order came into force on 1 February 2021.
events.why: A cooker without the ISI mark can no longer legally be sold in India.

events.title: A new edition of the standard
events.text: BIS published the seventh revision of IS 2347. It keeps the rule that the fusible safety plug must go before 3 kgf/cm², and treats a gasket release system as an extra layer that needs another safety device alongside.
events.why: The safety rules keep up with new cooker designs.

people.name: Denis Papin
people.note: Invented the steam digester and its weighted safety valve, and built the first piston steam model.

people.name: Nicolas Appert
people.note: Showed that food sealed and heated keeps for years, and published the method in 1810.

people.name: Charles Chamberland
people.note: Built the steam autoclave in Pasteur's laboratory to sterilise with steam above 100 °C.

people.name: José Alix Martínez
people.note: Patented the olla exprés in 1918 and wrote the first pressure-cooker recipe book.

people.name: Alfred Vischer
people.note: Patented a rubber blow-out safety plug for home cookers, filed in 1938.

people.name: H. D. Vasudeva
people.note: Founded the company that became Hawkins Cookers in 1959.

facts: Papin's 1682 supper for the Royal Society included bones cooked as soft as cheese, according to John Evelyn's diary.
The word autoclave means roughly 'self-locking': the steam pressure holds the door shut.
Steam pushes on a cooker's lid with a force like 380 kg standing on it, yet a 70 g weight on a 3 mm hole holds it back.
A cooker in Leh reaches only about 114 °C, because its weight adds the same pressure to much thinner air.
In the US, home canning of low-acid food has been done under pressure since the 1910s, because boiling water cannot kill botulinum spores.
